newsitem.title: PANAMA: No firing tests on U.S. weapons in Panama - military.
newsitem.headline: No firing tests on U.S. weapons in Panama - military.

text.p: The United States carried out exposure tests on nuclear and chemical weapons in Panama in the early 1990s to observe their performance under tropical conditions, a U.S. military official said on Wednesday.

"The shells were brought down here for exposure tests to this climate in a controlled environment and then sent back to the U.S.," Col. Byron Conover, spokesman at the U.S. military's Southern Command (Southcom), told Reuters.
He said the shells, after being exposed to tropical conditions, were then taken back to the United States and some were fired to examine whether the humidity and heat had brought about changes.
"But to our knowledge they were not fired down here," Conover said.
Conover said that during a six-month period from late 1993 to early 1994 about 70 depleted uranium shells were brought to Panama for testing.
Tests on low-grade nerve gas shells (Virex) were also brought to Panama in the mid-1960s before being sent back to the United States, he said.
Panama's government late on Tuesday said no evidence existed to show that the U.S. military had carried out tests on chemical and nuclear shells in Panama.

"Since the end of the Second World War until the present day the Foreign Ministry has not given any authorisation to the U.S. military or any third party to carry out any kind of tests on dangerous armaments on Panamanian territory," the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
"No civil or military body of the U.S. government has asked for authorisation from the Republic of Panama to carry out these types of tests," the Foreign Ministry added.
Conover did not say whether the Panamanian government had known about the tests on nuclear shells.
Local newspapers have carried reports recently of U.S. military tests at Panama bases leaving areas contaminated with chemical and nuclear wastes.

The Panama-based Southcom, which controls all U.S. military activity and national security interests in Latin America south of Mexico, will be transferred to Miami in September. In June it will also assume responsibility for the Caribbean.
In accordance with bilateral treaties, the United States will withdraw all troops and turn over control of the Panama Canal by Dec. 31, 1999.
